content:
Week 9 - Deploy the troops#What did I add this week?
This week I continued developing the exercise functionality in the REST API. I created an initial library of 40 predefined exercises and connected them to the newly created body parts in the database. Each exercise has a name, description and one or more associated body parts. The body parts also have colors, which can be used by the frontend when displaying exercises and training information when that time comes.
I implemented seeders for body parts and exercises so that the predefined data is inserted automatically when the application starts. The seeders check whether entries already exist before inserting them, allowing the initial library to be created without duplicating entries every time the application restarts.
I also improved the exercise API responses. Previously, the exercise DTO only contained the exercise ID, name and description. I extended it to include a list of body parts, including each body part’s ID, name and color. This gives the frontend the information it needs without requiring separate requests for every exercise’s body parts.
During this work, I encountered a Hibernate lazy-loading problem. The exercise’s body parts were loaded lazily, but the EntityManager was closed before the service converted the exercise into a DTO. I fixed this in the DAO queries by fetching the associated body parts together with the exercise. I applied this to both the query returning the available exercises and the query retrieving an individual exercise.
I also continued verifying the distinction between predefined exercises and custom exercises. Predefined exercises are shared between users, while custom exercises belong to their creator. The intention is that users can access the shared library and their own custom exercises without being able to modify another user’s private exercises.
Another important part of the week was verifying and deploying the backend. I inspected the Docker Compose configuration and Caddyfile on my DigitalOcean Droplet. This helped me identify that the API is served through the subdomain api.oniscidea.dk, with Caddy forwarding requests to the Java application on port 7070.
The application runs on a DigitalOcean Droplet using Docker, with the application image stored in Docker Hub and the source code hosted on GitHub. I reviewed the Docker Compose configuration to understand how PostgreSQL, Caddy and Watchtower work together. Caddy acts as a reverse proxy, handling HTTPS requests for api.oniscidea.dk and forwarding them to the Javalin application on port 7070, while Watchtower checks for updated container images.
I then tested the deployed API and confirmed that the body-parts endpoint returns all 14 predefined body parts. I also logged in to the deployed application, obtained a fresh JWT and successfully retrieved the exercise library using the authenticated exercises endpoint.
Which new technology did I use?
I continued using Hibernate/JPA to manage relationships between exercises and body parts. In particular, I used JPQL fetch joins to load related entities before the EntityManager is closed, avoiding lazy-loading exceptions when building DTOs.
I continued using DTOs to control the structure of the API responses. The updated ExerciseDTO now includes a list of BodyPartDTO objects, allowing the API to return structured exercise and body-part information in a single response.
I also worked with database seeders to populate the initial exercise library and body-part data. This separates the predefined application data from manual database setup and makes it easier to initialize the database consistently.
For deployment, I deployed my Digital Ocean droplet through Ubuntu, and made a Docker Compose setup, the Caddy reverse proxy and Watchtower. I also tested the production API using PowerShell and Invoke-RestMethod, including sending a JWT in the Authorization header.
Why did I structure it this way?
I wanted to create a reusable exercise library that the application can use when users plan their training. By connecting exercises to body parts, the API can provide the frontend with information that can be used for filtering, categorization and visual presentation.
I used seeders because predefined data should be available automatically when the application is initialized.
I extended the DTO rather than returning the Hibernate entity directly. This keeps the API response separate from the internal database model and gives the frontend the information it needs in a proper format.
The fetch joins were necessary because the service converts entities into DTOs after the DAO has completed its database operation. Fetching the body parts as part of the query ensures that the required relationship is loaded before the EntityManager closes.
For deployment, I wanted to verify that the backend works outside my local development environment. Testing the live API with a valid JWT confirmed that the deployed application can authenticate a user and return protected exercise data.
What worked well?
The initial exercise library was successfully created with 40 predefined exercises linked to the 14 body parts. The database contains the expected relationships between exercises and body parts.
Both exercise endpoints now return the body-part information in their responses. The lazy-loading issue was resolved by updating the DAO queries, and all 43 automated tests passed after these changes.
I also confirmed that the deployed backend is reachable over HTTPS at https://api.oniscidea.dk. The body-parts endpoint returned all 14 body parts, and the authenticated exercise endpoint returned 40 exercises after logging in and obtaining a fresh JWT.
This provided a useful check that the deployment, authentication, database seed data and exercise API work together in the production environment.
What was difficult or confusing?
One challenge was the lazy-loading behavior in Hibernate. The exercise endpoints initially returned HTTP 500 errors because the body-part collection was accessed after the EntityManager had closed. I needed to understand where the data was being loaded and update the DAO queries so that the relationship was fetched in time.
Another challenge was distinguishing between the different parts of the deployment. GitHub stores the source code, Docker Hub stores the container image, and the DigitalOcean Droplet runs the application using Docker. Caddy handles incoming HTTPS requests and forwards them to the Java backend, while Watchtower can update the running container when a new image is available.
I also initially confused the Google OAuth configuration with the hosting configuration. The Google web application controls OAuth permissions and redirect settings; it does not host the Java backend. Understanding this distinction helped me identify the actual production API URL.
What would I improve next time?
Next, I want to complete the final review of the backend before hand-in. I will focus on verifying that the main API flows work together correctly, checking error handling and input validation, and confirming that the deployed application continues to work after a restart.
I also want to review the deployment configuration, particularly environment variables, database exposure and the handling of credentials. The Google Calendar integration still needs to be checked against the production domain to ensure that its OAuth redirect URI and token handling work correctly.
Finally, I want to review the README and ensure that the project can be built, configured and started using the documented instructions. The goal is to finish with a backend that is not only functional but also straightforward for another developer or examiner to understand.
title: Training Program Week 9

content:
Week 8 - Reviewing API Flows, Expanding Security Tests and Integrating Google Calendar.#What did I add this week?
This week I continued improving the REST API by reviewing the existing API flows and checking that the different resources work together correctly. I looked at how users, profiles, training programs, training calendars, training sessions, exercise logs and set logs depend on each other.
I also worked on the security and integration tests. I added Cucumber step definitions for set log security, covering scenarios where a user creates or retrieves their own set logs and attempts to access resources belonging to another user. The test setup creates users, logs them in, obtains JWTs and creates the related profiles, calendars, training programs and training sessions needed for the scenarios.
I reviewed the API routes and how authentication is applied to them, including which endpoints must remain public and which require a valid JWT. I also continued checking the flow from creating a training program and scheduling a training session to recording exercises and sets.
Another change was updating the normal Hibernate configuration from create to update. This allows existing database data to remain in place when the application restarts, while the test EntityManagerFactory continues to use create for test setup.
Finally, I continued implementing Google Calendar integration. I wired the OAuth service, calendar service, connection DAO and controllers into the application and added routes for starting the connection, handling the callback, and creating, updating and deleting Google Calendar events.
*Which new technology did I use?
I continued using Cucumber, Gherkin, Rest Assured and JUnit to test the API through HTTP requests. The tests use the test server on port 7071 and exercise the API in a way that resembles how a client would use it.
I continued working with JWT authentication and authorization, particularly how tokens are passed between requests and how resources should be restricted to their owners.
For Google Calendar, I used Google’s OAuth 2.0 flow and the Google API client libraries. The application redirects the user to Google for authorization and then receives an authorization code through the callback. The application must exchange that code for tokens before it can access the user’s calendar.
I also continued using Hibernate/JPA and PostgreSQL, adjusting the database configuration to make local development easier without recreating the database schema on every normal application startup.
Why did I structure it this way?
I wanted to make sure that the API works as a connected system rather than as a collection of individual endpoints. For example, a training session depends on a training calendar and a training program, while exercise logs depend on training sessions and set logs depend on exercise logs. Testing these relationships helps verify that the complete flow works correctly.
I also wanted the security tests to create their own users and related data. This makes it possible to test ownership by using separate JWTs and checking whether one user can access another user’s resources.
The DAO, service and controller structure remains important because it separates database access, application logic and HTTP handling. I followed the same structure for Google Calendar so that the external integration fits into the existing application.
For database configuration, using update during normal startup prevents the application from unnecessarily recreating the schema and losing local development data. The test configuration remains separate so that tests can use a clean database setup.
What worked well?
The API’s main resource flows are in place, and I expanded the test setup to cover more of the relationships between users, calendars, training sessions, exercise logs and set logs.
I also made progress on the security tests for set logs, including setting up separate users and JWTs to test access to resources owned by different users.
The database configuration now supports preserving existing data during normal application restarts.
For Google Calendar, I successfully reached Google’s authorization pages and completed the consent flow in the browser. The application generates the authorization URL and receives the callback, which means the initial redirect and consent stages are working far enough to reach the token exchange.
What was difficult or confusing?
One challenge was reviewing the complete API flow and making sure that the test data is created in the correct order. Since the resources depend on each other, a test for a set log needs a user, a profile, a training calendar, a training program, a training session and an exercise log before the set log can be created.
Another challenge was making sure that authentication and authorization are handled correctly throughout the API. A valid JWT identifies the user, but the application must also verify that the user is allowed to access the requested resource.
The main unresolved problem is Google OAuth. After completing Google’s consent flow, the callback fails when exchanging the authorization code for tokens. Google’s token endpoint returns HTTP 401 Unauthorized, and the application returns HTTP 500. I added diagnostic logging, but the response body is currently reported as null, so the exact cause has not yet been confirmed.
What would I improve next time?
First, I want to finish reviewing the remaining API flows and security rules, particularly access to user-owned resources such as training programs, calendars, sessions, notes and logs. I also want to make sure that the existing tests cover the important successful and rejected requests without adding unnecessary complexity.
Next, I want to resolve the Google OAuth problem by checking that the client ID and client secret belong to the same OAuth client and that the registered redirect URI matches the application’s configuration.
Once the Google connection works, I will verify that the connection is saved correctly for the authenticated user and that the application can create, update and delete events in Google Calendar.
After that, I want to verify token refreshing and complete the end-to-end integration. The main goal is to ensure that the API’s existing training calendar functionality and the external Google Calendar integration work reliably together.
title: Training Program Week 8

content:
Week 7 - Implementing JWT Authentication and Authorization.#What did I add this week?
This week I focused on implementing JWT authentication and authorization in the REST API. I created a JwtService to generate and validate JSON Web Tokens and connected it to the existing login functionality. When a user successfully logs in, the API now returns a token along with the user’s basic information.
I also created JWT authentication middleware for Javalin. This middleware checks whether a request contains a valid bearer token before allowing access to protected endpoints.
After implementing authentication, I added authorization checks for profiles. Users can retrieve, update and delete their own profiles, but they receive a forbidden response if they try to access or modify a profile belonging to another user.
I also expanded the Cucumber security tests to cover these scenarios. All 15 Cucumber scenarios are now passing.
Which new technology did I use?
I used the JJWT library to generate and validate JSON Web Tokens. The tokens contain the user’s ID and email, and they expire after one hour. I also configured a secret key in my local configuration file to sign and validate the tokens.
I continued using Cucumber, Gherkin, Rest Assured and Testcontainers to test the API. I added scenarios for missing tokens, invalid tokens, accessing a user’s own profile, and attempting to access, update or delete another user’s profile.
Why did I structure it this way?
I wanted to separate authentication from authorization. Authentication verifies that a request has a valid token, while authorization checks whether the authenticated user is allowed to access a specific resource.
The JWT middleware handles token validation, while the profile service checks whether the requested profile belongs to the authenticated user. This keeps the ownership checks in the service layer and prevents the application from relying only on the client to enforce access restrictions.
I also kept the JWT secret outside the source code so that it does not need to be committed to version control.
What worked well?
The biggest success was getting JWT authentication integrated with the existing login endpoint and Javalin application. A user can log in, receive a token and use it to access protected profile endpoints.
I also successfully implemented ownership checks for retrieving, updating and deleting profiles. The automated tests verify that requests without a token or with an invalid token are rejected, and that users cannot access or modify another user’s profile.
All 15 Cucumber scenarios pass, including the new security tests. The tests continue to run against PostgreSQL using Testcontainers.
What was difficult or confusing?
One challenge was understanding the difference between authentication and authorization. Validating a token confirms which user is making the request, but it does not automatically mean that the user should have access to every resource.
I had to make sure that the authenticated user’s ID was available to the profile service so it could check ownership before performing operations. I also needed to extend the existing tests to verify both successful access and rejected requests.
What would I improve next time?
The security implementation is still incomplete because only the individual profile endpoints currently have authentication and ownership checks.
Next, I want to extend these checks to training programs, training calendars, notes and other user-owned resources. I also need to review profile creation and the endpoint that returns all profiles to ensure that users cannot access other users’ data through those routes.
After that, I want to add more automated security tests and verify the Google Calendar integration end to end.
title: Training Program Week 7

content:
Week 6 - Testing the API.#What did I add this week?
This week I continued working on the REST API and focused on getting the different parts of the application working together. I reviewed the controllers and worked on the main application setup so that I could start the application in tests without changing the normal configuration.
I also set up automated API testing using Cucumber, Gherkin, Rest Assured and Testcontainers. This allows me to test the API by sending actual HTTP requests to the application while using a temporary PostgreSQL database.
I created Cucumber scenarios for creating users, profiles, training programs, training calendars and training sessions. All of these tests are now passing.
Which new technology did I use?
I started using Cucumber and Gherkin to write tests in a format that describes what the application should do in plain language. I used Rest Assured to send HTTP requests and check the responses from the API.
I also used Testcontainers to run PostgreSQL in a container during testing. This means the tests can use a real PostgreSQL database instead of relying on a separate manually configured test database.
I updated the Hibernate test configuration so that I could connect the test application to the database created by Testcontainers.
Why did I structure it this way?
I wanted to test the application through the same HTTP endpoints that a client would use instead of only testing individual methods. This helps verify that the controllers, services, DAOs, Hibernate and database work together correctly.
Using Testcontainers also makes the testing setup more independent from my normal development database. Cucumber lets me describe the expected behaviour in a readable way, which makes it easier to understand what each test is checking.
What worked well?
The biggest success was getting the Cucumber API tests working with Rest Assured, Javalin, Hibernate and PostgreSQL. I now have passing scenarios for creating users, profiles, training programs, training calendars and training sessions.
I also managed to resolve some issues along the way. One issue was that the training calendar endpoint used a different route than I initially expected. Another was handling Java date and time values in JSON and adjusting the test to correctly check the date returned by the API.
It was useful to see how the different parts of the application work together in a real request rather than only checking them separately.
What was difficult or confusing?
Getting the testing environment set up was more complicated than writing the individual scenarios. I had to make sure that Testcontainers, Hibernate and Javalin all used the same test database and that the test application could start and stop correctly.
I also had to understand how JSON responses represent Java date and time values, since the date was returned as an array rather than the string format I expected.
What would I improve next time?
Next, I want to continue adding tests for the more important relationships in the application, especially exercises connected to training programs and the logging of completed training sessions.
I also want to review the security part of the application when we cover it in the course. After that, I can continue checking the Google Calendar integration and clean up the project before finishing the documentation.
title: Training Program Week 6

content:
Week 5 - Building the API.#What did I add this week?
This week I started building the actual REST API for the project. I created DAOs, services and controllers for the different parts of the training system, including users, profiles, training programs, exercises, training sessions, calendars, exercise logs, set logs, notes and body parts.
I also started working on the relationships between the entities, for example connecting exercises to training programs and exercises to body parts. I set up the routes in Javalin so that the different parts of the application can be accessed through API endpoints.
I also began setting up the Google Calendar integration. I updated the Google Calendar connection entity and DAO, as well as services for Google OAuth and interacting with the Google Calendar API.
Which new technology did I use?
I worked more with Javalin for creating the REST API and used DAO, service and controller layers to structure the application.
I also started using the Google Calendar API and Google OAuth for connecting the application to a user’s Google Calendar. I used Google’s Java libraries to handle authentication and calendar events.
Why did I structure it this way?
I wanted to separate the different responsibilities of the application instead of putting everything into the entities or controllers. The DAOs handle the database, the services contain the actual logic, and the controllers handle the HTTP requests.
This also makes it easier to add more functionality later without having one large class responsible for everything.
For Google Calendar, I wanted to keep the local database as the main part of the application while using Google Calendar as an external service that the application can communicate with.
What worked well?
I feel like the project has started to become an actual application rather than just a collection of entities. Having the different routes, services and controllers makes it much easier to see how the different pieces connect.
I also liked being able to build the project one resource at a time. Once I had one working structure, I could use the same general idea for the other resources and slowly build the API up.
What was difficult or confusing?
There are a lot of different layers and classes now, and sometimes it can be difficult to remember which responsibility belongs where. I also found the relationships between the entities more complicated once I started actually implementing them instead of just planning them.
The Google Calendar integration was also more confusing because it introduced OAuth, access tokens, refresh tokens and callback URLs, which are quite different from the normal CRUD functionality I had been working with.
What would I improve next time?
I would like to spend more time understanding the flow between the controller, service and DAO instead of just getting the code to work. I also want to understand the Google OAuth process better, especially how the authorization flow and state work, so that I understand what is happening instead of just following the structure.
I would also like to become more comfortable with how the different entities and their relationships are handled by Hibernate.
title: Training Program Week 5

I expanded upon the base I had already laid from last week. I expanded some of my entities and DAO’s for password hashing. To that I also made my DTO’s and tested all of it together with a small test set up in main to see all the data of a user got sent properly to the database.
I also expanded my work on getting the Google Calendar API and set up a service as well as an Authitication service.
I built a threadpool executor that will handle Google Calendar API calls while data is being sent to the database for smoother operations.
Which new technology did I use?
I have continued to read into and integrate a RESTful API.
I have also created a threadpool executor.
Why did I structure it this way?
It is time to begin to actually connect the various code bits and see if they can connect, and if they can connect in a way I want them to. Pulling the threads together into one, so to speak.
What worked well?
I have made progress in sending data into the database and seeing it be created as it should. Full testing on this matter still needs to be done.
What was difficult or confusing?
I am still working on fully integrating the Google Calendar API. I have all the parts that needs to be there, I just need to test it fully to the extend where I can see it works as intended.
What would I improve next time?
There is very little I would improve this week. I feel like I have gotten around to the things I nedeed to.

content:
Week 1 - Setting up shop.#What did I add this week?
I set up the basic structure for the projekt in paper format. I began writing down entities and forming up the idea around the project of what I wanted it to be.
I asked my clients about what they wanted the application to have of functionalities as well as what they might have of “nice to have” functions besides the MVP (minimal viable product), depending on how much time I would have left at the end of the project.
I began making and working on a domain model over the application as well as deciding on a name for the application: Oniscidea.
Which new technology did I use?
I used good old fashioned paper to put all my ideas of the project, as well as my clients needs and ideas down into one collection. From there I could work on the ideas and form a picture of where the project should head.
Why did I structure it this way?
I prefer knowing what I go into before I start anything. As many details and set in stone things as I could make, the better.
While I need to leave some things open to be able to scope and work on it, I do prefer to get certain things down before even starting to touch any code.
What worked well?
My clients had a lot of ideas and wishes for funtionality of the application. To this working in a structured and with open communication has put me in a good starting position.
I am always tryin to think three steps ahead, so I have already instrected my clients to think ahead of what they might want from the front end as well as specific other details I might need from them in the future.
What was difficult or confusing?
Diving into new terms, code syntax and having no idea how it really works together yet is always demanding.
What would I improve next time?
I would wish I had prepared better for school start in the summer vacation. Summer vacation and getting back from it is always.
I am having problems attending enough days, so I have to compensate by doing a lot of research on my own and having been a bit unsure on some of the technical things.
